We present and compare with multiple baselines: Traditional stylometry. We present a weak baseline (Ikae, 2021) from traditional stylometry. We represent input document pairs as the concatenation of their TF-IDF or word-count features, and train a Support Vector Machine (Cortes and Vapnik, 1995) to classify their shared authorship status (hyperparameters in Appendix E). Zero-shot, prior work. We present three zero-shot baselines with GPT-4-TURBO (temperature 0.0) and LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT (greedy decoding). The first baseline is chain-of-thought CoT (Wei et al., 2022), a standard self-rationalization method that does not include any Av specific instructions. The second baseline is PROMPTAV (Hung et al., 2023). We use the prompts for CoT and PROMPTAV reported in Hung et al. (2023) (Appendix C). Both these baselines report confidence scores (0-1, higher score means more confidence in shared authorship) in lieu of labels. We extract this confidence score by string matching for decimal numbers in the output; we measure accuracy by thresholding these scores at 0.5. Consistency cannot be calculated for these two baselines. The third zero-shot baseline is PROMPT-CAVE itself. Fine-tuned. Bias propagation from GPT-4-TURBO to CAVE, and mitigation: Since there is no human-written explanation data for Av, we used silver data generated by GPT-4-TURBO; however, this can lead to biases $^{13}$ present in GPT-4-TURBO to unconsciously propagate to CAVE. The datasets we use in this paper are not highly bias-prone; however, researchers/users who use our framework on their dataset might deal with biases that stem from their dataset (such as gender bias, racial bias, etc., for example: 'Document-1's writing style is depictive of demographic-X whereas Document-2's writing style is depictive of demographic-Y'). For users dealing with sensitive data for Av, we recommend they use bias mitigation strategies from relevant literature such as Counterfactual Role Reversal (Gupta et al., 2022) for gender bias, reducing bias in the upstream model before fine-tuning (UBM (Jin et al., 2021), strategic pretraining (Feng et al., 2023)), ensembling models with varying/opposing biases (partisan ensemble (Feng et al., 2023)), etc.

Hallucination. As we see in our human study, CAVE's rationales sometimes have hallucinated details, especially for certain linguistic features. Hallucination is a common problem faced when using LMs (Ji et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023); prior works (Zhang et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2024) have proposed task-specific strategies to alleviate the same. In our work, our proposed output format for CAVE allows for downstream users to analyze each linguistic feature independently, making it easier to identify hallucinations. We caution users to be aware of this issue, and to always manually read and verify the rationales before using them.

Completeness of rationale. We would like to emphasize here that our models have not been explicitly trained for completeness; that is, apart from any wrong information the generated explanation may have, it could also have missed some crucial similarity/dissimilarity between the documents. We discuss rationale properties such as completeness in Appendix K.

Trust. Lipton (2018) discusses that the definition of trust in a model is subjective: some users only trust well-understood models; other users might be inclined to trust well-performing mod

els regardless of how (not) explainable they are. A recent work Sun et al. (2024) defines various dimensions for trust for language models, such as truthfulness, safety, robustness, etc. Our improvements in terms of accessibility of rationales and automatic quality evaluation contribute to improved trust in certain dimensions; as future work, we would like to evaluate and improve on other dimensions of trust, including higher accuracy, more datasets, more OOD evaluation, etc.

Practical limitations. Lastly our method has practical limitations faced by any NLP task; our models are restricted by the size of the context window allowed by the model (both input and output text) (also keeping in mind restrictions due to computational costs, financial costs and GPU size available). This can lead to data missed by the model in its reasoning.

Data. All the datasets that we use in our work are released publicly for usage and have been duly attributed to their original authors. Note that while we perform authorship verification, all the datasets we use have been anonymized by their respective creators. We do not have access to or use the names of individual people.

For all our experiments, we report (1) the complete hyperparameter setting and any bounds explored (Appendix E) as well as the sizes and versions/pretrained-model links of all models used, (2) the time taken per experiment, and infrastructure used, (3) descriptions of datasets, and demonstrations used to sample rationales from GPT-4-TURBO. Further, we have released all our codes and our training/test data at github.com/INK-USC/Controllable-AV-Explanations.

LLAMA-3 Usage and License. Note that we were granted access to download and use LLAMA-3-8B from https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B. While we train a local LLAMA-3-8B, we do not release the trained model; we submit only the script and data used to train the model. Also note that we adhere to the intended use case for LLAMA-3-8B, i.e., "Llama 3 is intended for commercial and research use in English. Instruction tuned models are intended for assistant-like chat, whereas pretrained models can be adapted for a variety of natural language generation tasks."

We download the pre-trained LLAMA-3-8B from HuggingFace (https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B) and train it for all our experiments. We train it with Low-Rank Adaption (LoRA; Hu et al., 2021), a parameter-efficient training method which offers lightweight training no additional inference latency, unlike other existing parameter-efficient methods (Houlsby et al., 2019). We train LLAMA-3-8B for 10 epochs. We use no validation set, and instead use the last checkpoint obtained from training; since we have no gold-standard explanations,

we opt against using the GPT-4-TURBO generated data as the validation set. We experiment with different values of 'r' and 'alpha' for LoRA (refer to https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/main/en/conceptual Guides/lora for their definitions). We use $r = 128$ and alpha $= 256$ . Note that all our training experiments for LLAMA-3-8B take $\sim 12$ hours, and all our test set inferences take $\sim 7 - 8$ hours on a single NVIDIA Quadro RTX 8000 GPU. We report single-run results for all our experiments.

Why not LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT for fine-tuning? As explained in the documentation for LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT in hugging-face https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct, "Instruction tuned models are intended for assistant-like chat, whereas pretrained models can be adapted for a variety of natural language generation tasks". Hence, we provide zero-shot and few-shot baselines with LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT whereas we provide fine-tuned results on LLAMA-3-8B.

We present and compare with multiple baselines: Traditional stylometry. We present a weak baseline (Ikae, 2021) from traditional stylometry. We represent input document pairs as the concatenation of their TF-IDF or word-count features, and train a Support Vector Machine (Cortes and Vapnik, 1995) to classify their shared authorship status (hyperparameters in Appendix E). Zero-shot, prior work. We present three zero-shot baselines with GPT-4-TURBO (temperature 0.0) and LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT (greedy decoding). The first baseline is chain-of-thought CoT (Wei et al., 2022), a standard self-rationalization method that does not include any Av specific instructions. The second baseline is PROMPTAV (Hung et al., 2023). We use the prompts for CoT and PROMPTAV reported in Hung et al. (2023) (Appendix C). Both these baselines report confidence scores (0-1, higher score means more confidence in shared authorship) in lieu of labels. We extract this confidence score by string matching for decimal numbers in the output; we measure accuracy by thresholding these scores at 0.5. Consistency cannot be calculated for these two baselines. The third zero-shot baseline is PROMPT-CAVE itself. Fine-tuned. Bias propagation from GPT-4-TURBO to CAVE, and mitigation: Since there is no human-written explanation data for Av, we used silver data generated by GPT-4-TURBO; however, this can lead to biases $^{13}$ present in GPT-4-TURBO to unconsciously propagate to CAVE. The datasets we use in this paper are not highly bias-prone; however, researchers/users who use our framework on their dataset might deal with biases that stem from their dataset (such as gender bias, racial bias, etc., for example: 'Document-1's writing style is depictive of demographic-X whereas Document-2's writing style is depictive of demographic-Y'). For users dealing with sensitive data for Av, we recommend they use bias mitigation strategies from relevant literature such as Counterfactual Role Reversal (Gupta et al., 2022) for gender bias, reducing bias in the upstream model before fine-tuning (UBM (Jin et al., 2021), strategic pretraining (Feng et al., 2023)), ensembling models with varying/opposing biases (partisan ensemble (Feng et al., 2023)), etc.

Hallucination. As we see in our human study, CAVE's rationales sometimes have hallucinated details, especially for certain linguistic features. Hallucination is a common problem faced when using LMs (Ji et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023); prior works (Zhang et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2024) have proposed task-specific strategies to alleviate the same. In our work, our proposed output format for CAVE allows for downstream users to analyze each linguistic feature independently, making it easier to identify hallucinations. We caution users to be aware of this issue, and to always manually read and verify the rationales before using them.

Completeness of rationale. We would like to emphasize here that our models have not been explicitly trained for completeness; that is, apart from any wrong information the generated explanation may have, it could also have missed some crucial similarity/dissimilarity between the documents. We discuss rationale properties such as completeness in Appendix K.

Trust. Lipton (2018) discusses that the definition of trust in a model is subjective: some users only trust well-understood models; other users might be inclined to trust well-performing mod

els regardless of how (not) explainable they are. A recent work Sun et al. (2024) defines various dimensions for trust for language models, such as truthfulness, safety, robustness, etc. Our improvements in terms of accessibility of rationales and automatic quality evaluation contribute to improved trust in certain dimensions; as future work, we would like to evaluate and improve on other dimensions of trust, including higher accuracy, more datasets, more OOD evaluation, etc.

Practical limitations. Lastly our method has practical limitations faced by any NLP task; our models are restricted by the size of the context window allowed by the model (both input and output text) (also keeping in mind restrictions due to computational costs, financial costs and GPU size available). This can lead to data missed by the model in its reasoning.

Data. All the datasets that we use in our work are released publicly for usage and have been duly attributed to their original authors. Note that while we perform authorship verification, all the datasets we use have been anonymized by their respective creators. We do not have access to or use the names of individual people.

For all our experiments, we report (1) the complete hyperparameter setting and any bounds explored (Appendix E) as well as the sizes and versions/pretrained-model links of all models used, (2) the time taken per experiment, and infrastructure used, (3) descriptions of datasets, and demonstrations used to sample rationales from GPT-4-TURBO. Further, we have released all our codes and our training/test data at github.com/INK-USC/Controllable-AV-Explanations.
